```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.4, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
```

Most calibration problems start in the data. A rainfall series shifted by one time step, a
flow record in the wrong units or a gap filled with zeros will spoil a calibration, and no
amount of searching will put it right. This guide takes you from Environment Agency sources to
the three files pdmS7 reads, and ends with a checklist to run before every calibration.

# What pdmS7 expects

| File | Columns | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| `forcing.csv` | `time`, `rain`, `pet` | Rain and potential evaporation as **totals over the time step**, in mm. No gaps. |
| `flow.csv` | `q_m3s` (and optionally `time`) | **Mean** flow over the time step, in m3/s. Gaps left empty. |
| `basin.yml` | `area_km2`, `calibration`, and optional extras | Described in [Calibrating many catchments](many-catchments.html) |

Three conventions matter more than any other:

- **Time stamps mark the end of the step.** The row stamped 10:00 holds the rain that fell from
  09:45 to 10:00, at 15 minutes, and the model's flow for the same quarter hour.
- **Times are UTC.** British Summer Time never appears in a model file.
- **The step is fixed.** Every row is one step after the last: 15 minutes, an hour or a day.

# Step 1: get the data with reach.io

[reach.io](https://github.com/JonPayneEA/reach.io) finds stations, downloads from the EA
Hydrology API, keeps a Bronze store of raw data with provenance, and promotes it to a Silver
store with quality flags. Use it rather than ad hoc downloads: every series then has a record of
where it came from, which the calibration log can point to.

```{r reach-io, eval=FALSE}
library(reach.io)
stations <- find_stations(lat = 51.5, long = -1.8, dist = 15)
got <- download_hydrology(
  parameters = c("rainfall", "flow"), from_date = "2010-01-01", to_date = "2024-12-31",
  wiski_ids = c("SS92F014", "S11512_FW"), method = "batch", output = "disk",
  out_dir = "data/hydrometric"
)
# Quality control: Bronze to Silver, with a qc_flag per reading.
promote_to_silver("data/hydrometric/bronze/hydrometric/EA/Q/2024/EA_39001_Q_20240101.parquet")
flow <- read_silver("data/hydrometric", "39001", "Q")
```

reach.io's `format_for_pdm()` writes the layout of the older PDM for PCs program, with separate
year, month and day columns. pdmS7 reads plain CSV files with one `time` column, as below.

# Step 2: use the quality flags

reach.io's Silver data carry a flag on every reading: 1 good, 2 estimated, 3 suspect,
4 rejected. A simple rule serves most calibrations:

| Flag | Flow | Rainfall |
|---|---|---|
| 1 good, 2 estimated | Keep | Keep |
| 3 suspect | Keep, and look at the worst periods by eye | Keep, and look at the worst periods by eye |
| 4 rejected | Set to missing | Set to missing, then infill (step 5) |

Missing flow is harmless: pdmS7 leaves it out of every score. Missing rain is not, because the
model cannot run through a gap in its inputs.

```{r flags}
flow <- data.frame(value = c(2.1, 2.3, 2.2, 0, 2.6), qc_flag = c(1, 1, 3, 4, 1))
flow$q_m3s <- ifelse(flow$qc_flag == 4, NA, flow$value)
flow
```

# Step 3: get the time stamps right

## Start or end of the step

Check how your source stamps its totals. If a 15-minute rainfall total is stamped at the
**start** of its quarter hour, every value must move one step later, or the model sees the rain
15 minutes early. That is a small shift, but it biases every timing score and every hindcast.

```{r shift}
start_stamped <- data.frame(
  time = as.POSIXct(c("2024-01-01 09:00", "2024-01-01 09:15", "2024-01-01 09:30"), tz = "UTC"),
  rain = c(0.2, 1.4, 0.6)
)
end_stamped <- transform(start_stamped, time = time + 15 * 60)
end_stamped
```

The test: plot rain and flow for a few sharp storms. Flow cannot rise before the rain that
causes it. If it appears to, the rain is stamped late or the flow early.

## Summer time

Data exported from some systems is in local time. In local time the last Sunday in October has
one hour twice and the last Sunday in March has one hour missing. Read such data with
`tz = "Europe/London"` and convert to UTC: the duplicated and missing hours then disappear.

```{r bst}
local <- as.POSIXct(c("2024-03-31 00:45", "2024-03-31 02:00"), tz = "Europe/London")
format(local, tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)
```

Local 00:45 and 02:00 on that night are only 15 minutes apart in UTC: the hour that never
happened has gone.

## A fixed step

Gaps in the time column itself, rather than missing values, break the fixed step. Fill them
with explicit rows:

```{r grid}
times <- as.POSIXct(c("2024-01-01 00:00", "2024-01-01 00:15", "2024-01-01 00:45"), tz = "UTC")
values <- c(1.0, 1.1, 1.3)
grid <- seq(min(times), max(times), by = 15 * 60)
full <- data.frame(time = grid, q_m3s = values[match(grid, times)])
full
```

# Step 4: units and step length

- **Rainfall** is already a depth per step. To change the step, add depths: four 15-minute
  totals make one hourly total.
- **Flow** is a rate. To change the step, average: four 15-minute flows make one hourly mean.
  pdmS7's `q_m3s` is a mean over the step, so compare it with the mean observed flow over the
  same step, not with an instantaneous reading at its end.
- **Levels** need a rating before they can be compared with modelled flow. Use reach.io's
  `apply_rating()` and keep the rating with the data. Treat flows above the highest gauged flow
  with caution; for warning thresholds set as levels, pdmS7's `register_data()` converts them
  through the rating and refuses levels outside it.

```{r aggregate}
quarter <- data.frame(rain = c(0.2, 1.4, 0.6, 0, 0.1, 0, 0, 0),
                      q_m3s = c(2.0, 2.1, 2.5, 3.0, 3.2, 3.1, 2.9, 2.8))
hour <- rep(1:2, each = 4)
data.frame(rain = tapply(quarter$rain, hour, sum), q_m3s = tapply(quarter$q_m3s, hour, mean))
```

# Step 5: catchment rainfall

The model needs the rain falling on the whole catchment, not at one gauge. reach.io returns
gauge series; combining them is your step. Three common choices:

| Method | When |
|---|---|
| A gridded radar-gauge product, averaged over the catchment | Best where available; captures storms between gauges |
| Gauge weights from Thiessen polygons, or from the share of catchment each gauge represents | A few gauges in or near the catchment |
| One gauge | Small catchments only; say so in the calibration's reasoning |

With fixed weights, a missing value at one gauge can be covered by re-weighting the others for
that step:

```{r weights}
gauges <- cbind(a = c(1.2, 0.8, NA, 0.0), b = c(1.0, 0.6, 0.9, 0.1), c = c(1.4, NA, 1.1, 0.0))
weights <- c(a = 0.5, b = 0.3, c = 0.2)
catchment_rain <- apply(gauges, 1, function(r) {
  ok <- !is.na(r)
  sum(r[ok] * weights[ok]) / sum(weights[ok])
})
round(catchment_rain, 3)
```

Infill rainfall once, by one recorded method, before any model sees it, and keep a note of which
steps were infilled. Never infill flow for scoring.

# Step 6: potential evaporation

PET has much less effect on floods than rainfall, but it controls how dry the soil gets in
summer, and so how big the first autumn floods are.

- Use a measured or modelled series (MORECS, MOSES or a Penman-Monteith calculation) where you
  have one.
- Otherwise reach.io's `fit_pe_sine()` and `generate_pe_sine()` give a smooth annual curve,
  reliable for UK lowland catchments.
- PET is a depth per step, like rain. Spread a daily value evenly across the day's steps
  (a daily total of 2.4 mm becomes 0.025 mm per 15 minutes), unless you have a diurnal pattern
  you trust.

```{r pet}
daily_pet <- 2.4
rep(daily_pet / 96, 3)
```

# Step 7: write the files

```{r write}
folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "B01")
dir.create(folder, showWarnings = FALSE)
time <- seq(as.POSIXct("2024-01-01 00:15", tz = "UTC"), by = 15 * 60, length.out = 8)
forcing <- data.frame(time = format(time, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), rain = quarter$rain,
                      pet = 0.025)
data.table::fwrite(forcing, file.path(folder, "forcing.csv"))
data.table::fwrite(data.frame(time = forcing$time, q_m3s = quarter$q_m3s),
                   file.path(folder, "flow.csv"))
writeLines(c("area_km2: 64", "calibration: [2024-01-01, 2024-01-02]"),
           file.path(folder, "basin.yml"))
cat(readLines(file.path(folder, "forcing.csv"), n = 3), sep = "\n")
```

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
unlink(folder, recursive = TRUE)
```

# The same steps with pdmS7's functions

Steps 3 to 7 recur for every catchment, and each script that rewrites them is a new chance to
misread a time column or a unit. pdmS7 has a function for each, and each one notes what it did
on the series it returns. When the data are registered, `register_data()` writes those notes
into the calibration log, so a reviewer sees, for example, that 412 steps of evaporation were
interpolated.

| Step | Function |
|---|---|
| Read an export: split year/month/day columns, one time column, or a date and a time column | `read_hydro_series()` |
| Put every series on one grid over the period they share | `align_series()` |
| Convert units: mm per hour or day, l/s, megalitres a day | `convert_units()` |
| Fill rain and evaporation gaps by a named rule, or stop and list them | `fill_gaps()` |
| Set negative rain to zero | `zero_negatives()` |
| Check totals, gaps, negatives and the runoff ratio | `check_inputs()` |

Here two exports in different layouts, one with a gap and one in litres a second, become
registered data:

```{r prepare}
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "exports")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
t <- seq(as.POSIXct("2024-01-01", tz = "UTC"), by = 900, length.out = 24 * 4 * 30)
set.seed(5)
rain <- ifelse(runif(length(t)) < 0.04, rexp(length(t), 1.5), 0)
rain[300:303] <- NA
lt <- as.POSIXlt(t)
write.csv(data.frame(year = lt$year + 1900, month = lt$mon + 1, day = lt$mday,
                     hours = lt$hour, minutes = lt$min, rainfall = rain),
          file.path(dir, "rain.csv"), row.names = FALSE, na = "")
wet <- ifelse(is.na(rain), 0, rain)
flow_ls <- 400 + as.numeric(stats::filter(wet, 0.995, method = "recursive")) * 60
write.csv(data.frame(Timestamp = format(t, "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M"), Value = flow_ls),
          file.path(dir, "flow.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

raw <- list(rain = read_hydro_series(file.path(dir, "rain.csv")),
            flow = read_hydro_series(file.path(dir, "flow.csv")))
raw$flow
grid <- align_series(rain = raw$rain, flow = raw$flow)
forcing <- data.frame(
  time = grid$time,
  rain = zero_negatives(fill_gaps(grid$rain, "zero", grid$time, "rain"), "rain"),
  pet = 0.02
)
flow <- convert_units(grid$flow, "ls", dt = 0.25, quantity = "flow")
check_inputs(forcing, flow, area_km2 = 40, ranges = list(rain = c(0, 1e4), pet = c(0, 1e4),
                                                         runoff_ratio = c(0.1, 0.9)))
```

The check prints what each step did. The ranges are opened up here only because the example is
a single month; for a real record keep the defaults, which suit the British Isles. A flag under
**CHECK** usually means the wrong units or the wrong area. `calibrate_project()` then takes the
prepared `forcing` and `flow` through registration, staged calibration, candidate, validation and
test in one call, with every step in the log.

```{r prepare-cleanup, include=FALSE}
unlink(dir, recursive = TRUE)
```

# The checklist

Run these before every calibration. Each takes a minute and each has caught a real error
somewhere. `check_inputs()` covers most of them in one call; the code below shows what it
checks, for data prepared some other way.

```{r checklist, eval=FALSE}
f <- data.table::fread("forcing.csv")
q <- data.table::fread("flow.csv")
f$time <- as.POSIXct(f$time, tz = "UTC")
stopifnot(nrow(f) == nrow(q))                       # the files line up
table(diff(as.numeric(f$time)))                     # one step length only
c(rain_missing = sum(is.na(f$rain)), pet_missing = sum(is.na(f$pet)))  # both zero
c(rain_negative = sum(f$rain < 0, na.rm = TRUE), pet_negative = sum(f$pet < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
mean(is.na(q$q_m3s))                                # share of flow missing
# Water balance: in a typical year, flow out should be less than rain in.
area_km2 <- 64
runoff_mm <- sum(q$q_m3s, na.rm = TRUE) * 900 / (area_km2 * 1000)  # 900 s per 15-min step
rain_mm <- sum(f$rain[!is.na(q$q_m3s)])
runoff_mm / rain_mm                                 # runoff ratio: well below 1
```

| Check | Expect | If not |
|---|---|---|
| Rows line up | Same number, same times | Re-join on time, not by position |
| One step length | A single value | Fill the grid (step 3) |
| Rain and PET missing | Zero | Infill rain (step 5); fill PET from a curve (step 6) |
| Negative values | Zero | A data fault; reach.io's QC flags most of these |
| Flow missing | Under 10 per cent in each period | Choose other periods, or note it |
| Runoff ratio | Below 1: about 0.2 in the dry south-east, 0.8 or more in the wet north and west | Wrong area, wrong units, or rain from the wrong place |
| Storm timing by eye | Flow rises after rain | Shift by one step (step 3) |

Then follow [Your first model run](example-workflow.html), or, for many catchments at once,
[Calibrating many catchments](many-catchments.html).
